lines.say: Remember turning the R Y knob by hand until a qubit, a quantum bit, read one a quarter of the time?
This time, let a computer turn it for you.
It's like tuning a guitar by ear: pluck, hear how far off it is, nudge the peg, pluck again.
Our circuit's pegs are its rotation angles, like theta, left free to change, so it's trainable.
Start theta at pi over two: a one comes up half the time, but we want a quarter.
How far off we are is called the cost. Plotted against theta, it's a valley with zero at the bottom.
Its slope, called the gradient, shows which way is downhill, so we nudge that way.
Run, measure, nudge again, and the chance slides from fifty percent to twenty five.
Each time, the new theta is the old theta minus a small step times the slope.
An ordinary program, the optimizer, runs this loop, just as AI models are trained.
But here the guitar picture breaks: you hear a pitch the moment you pluck.
Each run gives just a zero or a one, so we estimate the cost from many runs, called shots.
Even the slope must be measured, by rerunning with theta shifted pi over two each way.
So every listen costs many runs.
And quantum learning isn't automatically better: today it often matches ordinary computers, or does worse.
The point is knowing how it works, and where it might help.
So a trainable circuit has knobs, and an optimizer turns them downhill on a measured cost.
